title: The divine messengers
hook: Yama asks: didn't you see the baby, the old, the sick, the dead?

segments.voice: Yesterday: mountain shadows and your line, the turtle and the yoke. Did you do one thing you'd be glad to remember? Today, the very next discourse, and a judge who asks questions. Day four hundred ninety-eight.

A smoke alarm chirps. Low battery. You think: I'll deal with it later. It chirps again a week later. Again a week after that. Every chirp is a message, and none of them shouts. The hundred and thirtieth discourse imagines a person after death, brought before Yama, the king of the dead in Indian tradition. Yama doesn't open with a list of crimes. He asks questions. Good man, he says, didn't you see the first messenger of the gods when it appeared among people? And the person says: no, sir, I didn't. Today: the divine messengers.
screen: `A SMOKE ALARM CHIRPS.` → `BEFORE KING YAMA.` → `DIDN'T YOU SEE THE MESSENGER?`

segments.voice: Then Yama explains. Didn't you ever see a tiny baby, lying helpless in its own mess? And didn't it occur to you: I too was born; let me do good while I can? The second messenger: an old person, eighty, ninety, a hundred, bent like a roof beam, leaning on a stick, trembling. Didn't you think: I too will age? The third: someone sick, in pain, lifted and laid down by others. The fourth: someone caught for a crime and punished. The fifth: a dead body, a day or two or three gone. Five messengers, and each time Yama asks the same thing: didn't it occur to you that you are subject to this too? Then the line at the center. This harm, Yama says, wasn't done by your mother or father, your brother or sister, your friends, your relatives, or the gods. You did it, and you will feel its fruit. It's stern. But listen to who these messengers are. Not angels with trumpets. A baby. A grandparent. A patient. A body. They appear among ordinary people every day. Many Buddhists hear an echo here of the four sights that, in the traditional life story, moved young Siddhartha to leave the palace: an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering monk. And the discourse ends with a surprise: Yama himself wishes he could be born human, hear a Buddha teach, and understand. Even the judge of the dead wants the chance the living have.
screen: `A BABY, AN ELDER, SOMEONE SICK` · `THE PUNISHED AND THE DEAD` · `YOU DID IT, NOT THEM` · `EVEN YAMA WANTS THIS CHANCE` · then, large: `THE MESSENGERS CAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one messenger today. Sit and settle. Bring to mind someone you saw recently: an infant in a stroller, an older neighbor on the stairs, a friend who's ill. Let them be a messenger, not of fear, but of a plain fact: I'm a body too, and this time is limited. Let that make the next breath a little more awake. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
The divine messengers. Birth, aging, sickness, punishment and death, appearing among ordinary people, asking each of us: didn't you notice? Today's word.
Your line: the messengers came. Today, when you pass a baby, an elder or someone unwell, let it be a quiet message, and do one good thing while you can. Day four hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Buddhists often reflect on aging, sickness and death as everyday reminders to practice, and the four sights of the young Siddhartha are retold at festivals and in temple murals across Buddhist countries.

original.note: Pali devaduta: messenger of the gods. the title of MN 130.

trapdoor: what you thought: divine messengers are angels who bring announcements.
what it means: in MN 130 they're a baby, an elder, the sick, the punished and the dead, met every day.
what a scholar hears: MN 130, the Devaduta Sutta, has five messengers; the traditional biography's four sights (old, sick, dead, renunciant) overlap with them and are often read together.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 130, Devaduta Sutta (the divine messengers)
The four sights (traditional life of the Buddha; cf. Digha Nikaya 14 for Vipassi)

notes: MN 130 paraphrased. Confirm the five messengers in order and the description of the old person ('bent like a roof bracket').
The hell descriptions after Yama's questioning are omitted.
Confirm the closing: Yama's wish to be born human, meet a Tathagata and understand the teaching.
The link to the four sights is presented as what many Buddhists hear in it, not as a textual claim.
